participation.text: A political frame contains local autonomy and differing kinds of governance; it is not equivalent to every Sahelian community.

evidence.text: Oral poetry, texts, material remains and foreign images can disagree productively.

obligation.text: Royal wealth and wider exchange rested on productive work and unequal relationships. A foreign royal image is weak evidence for particular household obligations; archaeology and accounts must supply different tests.

name: Mali: pilgrimage, trade and historical voices
place: Western Sahel; locator at Timbuktu, Mali
geographicPrecision: Regional orientation at a scholarly/trade center, not a certain imperial capital or border.

interval.label: Mali political frame, c.1230–1600 CE
interval.note: Broad exhibition convention; political influence and local autonomy changed. This is not an exact founding or extinction date.

question: How do oral history, foreign images and material evidence change one another?
summary: Mali’s rulers depended on a landscape of farming, fishing, making and exchange. The resources displayed by a court came through many people’s work. Oral histories, excavated fragments and foreign depictions preserve different parts of that world. Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage is one dated episode within changing political networks, not the origin of West African urban life or its only important story.

sections.title: Begin below the royal throne
sections.text: The supplied atlas detail makes a seated ruler and a gold-colored object prominent. Ordinary work is largely absent. Berzock’s archaeological synthesis instead describes unglazed pots used for cooking, storing food and carrying commodities such as grain and fish. Iron tools, metalworking and regional exchange supported daily life. A rare imported fragment is striking, but the common broken vessel can be more direct evidence of repeated household tasks. Neither should be discarded because it lacks a royal name.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 26–29: domestic ceramics and materials

sections.title: Cities had histories before this empire
sections.text: Jenne-jeno developed long before the conventional Mali frame. Archaeology identifies a diverse urban population and specialized work without an obvious royal palace at its center. This challenges a story in which urban life arrived only with foreign traders or a named conquering king. It does not establish one uniform political system across all places later associated with Mali. A settlement’s local organization and an empire’s wider claims operate at different scales.

citations.locator: Ancient Mali and Middle Niger Civilization; Archaeology

sections.title: Exchange required relationships and could impose violence
sections.text: River-basin production and pastoral movement linked different environments. Saharan exchange added longer connections, including salt, cloth, metals and gold. Muslim merchants and scholars participated in relationships that also crossed religious differences. These were not exclusively equal or voluntary exchanges: enslaved people were transported through the same wider networks. Goods circulating and rulers prospering do not establish the security or freedom of all those doing the work.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 27–28: accounts, slavery and material evidence

sections.title: A pilgrimage and a later map have separate dates
sections.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo on pilgrimage in 1324. The atlas, conventionally dated about 1375 and attributed to Abraham Cresques, was made in Majorca. It presents him with a crown, a throne and gold. Those signs make wealth and rulership legible to a foreign court audience. They are not a portrait made from life, an inventory of his treasury or a neutral map of political boundaries. The image tells us how news of Mali could be selected and pictured elsewhere.

sections.title: Remembering also involved living work
sections.text: Mande jeliw have carried genealogies, praise and Sunjata narratives through performance. These living traditions changed with audiences and circumstances. They should not be treated as a single frozen transcript of the thirteenth century, or dismissed because they are oral. Compare their purposes with foreign accounts and archaeological contexts before deciding what a particular claim can establish.

deeperReading.title: An atlas is a made argument about the world
deeperReading.text: The supplied image is already a detail, not the whole atlas panel. Its larger ruler, gold, place signs and intersecting lines invite attention to particular resources and powers. Ask who made that selection and who could read it. The Block catalogue qualifies both the Cresques attribution and a possible royal commission. Keeping those qualifications does not make the image unusable: it makes an interpretation more precise. The accompanying text’s claim of extraordinary wealth belongs to the map, not to an audited modern ranking.

citations.locator: Foreign visual language, Mansa Musa section

deeperReading.title: Context changes what a fragment can say
deeperReading.text: A pot fragment with a documented excavation context can connect material, use and date. An object removed without a record loses part of that relationship. Berzock’s chapter places common wares alongside rare imports to avoid making distant commerce the whole economy. This does not let us assign every sherd to a Mali royal workshop. A regional archaeological assemblage and a named ruler’s reign must be joined by evidence, rather than by sharing a place on a modern map.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 27–29: fragmented sources and ceramic assemblages

deeperReading.title: A broad interval contains uneven changes
deeperReading.text: The case keeps its approximate 1230–1600 exhibition frame. It does not announce an exact foundation or sudden extinction. The rise of Songhay overlapped later Mali histories; every settlement did not change allegiance on a single year. Likewise, the Met’s exhibition labels Musa’s passage through Cairo in 1324, while its later interview describes the pilgrimage as 1325. Here 1324 remains the Cairo anchor; the source wording difference stays documented rather than silently replacing the original case date.

evidenceReading.title: Look for the people missing from the royal image
evidenceReading.introduction: A foreign depiction, living narratives and excavated material are compared without making one erase the others.

items.label: Crown and gold
items.text: The supplied detail gives the seated ruler a crown, staff and gold-colored round object.
items.interpretation: These are visible devices of royal representation, not measurements of personal wealth.

items.label: Pots and food
items.text: Berzock discusses unglazed vessels used in household and regional provisioning.
items.interpretation: Common material helps recover ordinary work. No particular potter or royal order is identified by the atlas.

items.label: A performed past
items.text: The museum account describes jeliw and continuing Sunjata performances.
items.interpretation: A living tradition has its own contexts and purposes; this dossier does not claim to have heard or translated a particular performance.

placeStudy.title: Niger-region settlements: older work and changing powers
placeStudy.description: Approximate settlement-area points distinguish Jenne-jeno, Timbuktu and Gao. They do not reconstruct a Mali capital, fixed boundary or caravan itinerary. Cairo and Majorca, named in the account, lie outside this regional view.

points.label: Jenne-jeno — older urban history
points.text: A deliberately rounded site-area locator for a long-lived settlement studied archaeologically. Its urban development preceded the selected Mali frame; no particular pot or workshop is pinpointed.

points.label: Timbuktu — scholarly and political histories
points.text: The exhibition links Musa’s return with Islamic study and later describes changing power. The point is not a certain imperial capital or a surveyed medieval outline.

points.label: Gao — distinct settlement and later power
points.text: A major exchange setting with histories before and beyond the Mali frame. Shared regional orientation does not make each settlement governed identically.
